opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the "billionth-best human" framing is useful as a rough intuition pump, but it has some real limitations.

The basic idea is that you want some reference point for how capable an AI is in a given domain, so you ask: if you lined up all humans, where would this system fall? If it's around the billionth-best, it's better than most people but nowhere near expert level. The problem is that this smooshes together a lot of different things.

First, the distribution of human ability is really weird and domain-dependent. In a lot of professional domains, the billionth-best human basically doesn't know how to do the task at all, because most people have never tried. So "better than the billionth-best person at writing a compiler" is mostly telling you the system has any competence at all, not where it sits relative to people who actually do the work. The gap between "can sort of do it" and "median professional" and "top professional" is where all the action is, and the population-ranking framing compresses that.

Second, AI capability profiles are really uneven in ways that don't map onto human profiles. Humans who are good at one part of a job tend to be good at related parts, because the skills are learned together. AIs can be superhuman at recalling obscure facts or writing boilerplate quickly while being much worse than a junior employee at something like noticing they've gone down a dead end, managing a long project, or checking their own work. So you can't summarize a model with a single rank, because it's at the 99.99th percentile on some sub-skills and below many humans on others, and what matters economically is often the weakest link.

Third, and relatedly, the thing I care most about is whether AIs can actually substitute for or accelerate the work of top experts, especially on AI R&D. For that, the relevant comparison isn't the general population at all, it's the best researchers and engineers at AI companies. The difference between a pretty good engineer and a top researcher at a frontier lab is huge in terms of impact, and a population-level ranking doesn't give you much resolution there.

Finally, there's the issue of cost and speed. An AI that's at some level of capability but runs at 50x human speed with many parallel copies is very different from a single human at that level. So even if you nail down the rank, you're missing a big part of what determines the actual impact.

So I'd say it's a fine way to communicate "these systems are already better than most people at lots of things," but if you're trying to forecast things like automation of AI research, you really want to compare against the relevant expert population, look at the full capability profile, and account for the speed and cost advantages.

r001.rationale: The response says most people have never attempted many professional tasks, so ranking a system against the billionth-best person mostly measures basic competence rather than meaningfully extending rankings among practitioners.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing I'd flag is that the billionth-best professional framing is really a statement about the distribution of human ability, and it kind of smuggles in an assumption that AI capability gaps look like human capability gaps. And I don't think that's true. When you take a human who's at, say, the 99.9th percentile versus the median, the profile of what they're good at and bad at is correlated in a fairly specific way — they're usually better across the board, with some bumps. AI systems have a really jagged profile. They might be superhuman at something like breadth of knowledge or speed at writing boilerplate code, and then fail at something a mediocre junior employee would handle fine, like keeping track of what they did over a multi-week project, or noticing that they've been going in circles for an hour.

So when you ask "is this system as good as the billionth-best human," the honest answer is often "it's much better on some dimensions and much worse on others, and there's no human it's actually comparable to." The reference point implicitly assumes a single axis, and the thing we're trying to measure isn't on a single axis.

The second issue is that the thing that matters for the questions I care about — like, when do we get systems that can substantially automate AI R&D, or when do things become dangerous — isn't really "how good is this compared to a typical professional." It's more like "can this thing do the full job end to end without a human in the loop." And a lot of what separates a working professional from current AI isn't raw intelligence in some narrow sense; it's stuff like reliability, agency over long horizons, handling the messy context of a real organization. A human who's genuinely at the billionth-best level in a field can be left alone for a month and come back with something. We don't currently have that, even from systems that would crush that same human on a lot of benchmarks.

So I think the framing is useful as a rough intuition pump — it does get at the point that most economically relevant work isn't done by the top 0.01%, and so AI doesn't need to be a genius to matter a lot. I'd defend that part. But I'd be careful about treating it as a threshold where you'd expect things to go from "not transformative" to "transformative." The more useful question to me is something like: what fraction of the tasks, weighted by economic value, can be handed off, and at what level of autonomy. And on that question the human-percentile framing can actually mislead you, because it'll tell you we're already there on the narrow benchmarks while we're clearly not there on the actual jobs.

r001.rationale: The response says AI has a jagged skill profile that cannot be reduced to a single human comparison, but it does not argue that professional rankings cannot be extrapolated beyond people pursuing that profession.

astra-6.text: Well, the billionth-best human at something generally isn’t a professional at it. There aren’t a billion professional programmers, for example. So you’re probably talking about someone who has essentially no experience in the domain, and their performance will depend a lot on how much training you give them. That makes it a pretty unclear reference point. And even if an AI is better than that person at every task, it could still have important weaknesses relative to the people who actually do those tasks professionally.

r001.rationale: The response says there may not be a billion professionals in a domain, so the billionth-ranked person would likely have almost no experience and would be an unclear benchmark.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main limitation is that it depends a lot on the task. For some tasks, there aren’t a billion humans who can do them at all, so the billionth-best human is basically someone who has no idea what they’re doing. And then being better than that doesn’t tell you very much about whether an AI could do the task competently.

More generally, human abilities are correlated in ways that AI abilities might not be. So an AI could be much better than almost everyone at some things and still have gaps that would seem surprising in a human with those strengths. You really want to ask which particular capabilities are needed for the work you care about, and whether the AI has those, rather than locate it at a single point on a human ranking.

r001.rationale: The response says some tasks have fewer than a billion people capable of doing them, making the billionth-best person effectively incompetent. This communicates that the benchmark becomes meaningless when extended beyond the relevant skilled population.
